stories.title: Things to know when you get cancer
stories.titleZh: 患癌症时需要了解的事情

comments.author: stochastician
comments.textRawHtml:
The second opinion advice is great, and what I tell everyone I know who gets cancer.

My mom was diagnosed with stage 1 cancer in 2006 in Idaho. I was a PhD student at MIT at the time and a friend in lab helped me get an appointment at Dana-Farber. I thought it was probably overkill (it was a common cancer) but we did it anyway. They said everything in Idaho was standard of care but suggested one extra test, which Idaho team then reluctantly did, which revealed distant metastasis (stage 4! ), dramatically changing her treatment trajectory. She lived another 15 years (I miss you Mom).

Asking for a second opinion sucks. A lot of us are preconditioned from birth to trust our clinicians. But you're going on a journey and your life (or the life of your loved one) is on the line. Insurance often covers it. Your doctor will NOT be offended.

Think of it this way : if you were deploying code to the mars rover, and your colleague asked to do a code review before you pushed go, would you be offended? This is even more important than that.
comments.textZhHtml:
第二意见建议很棒，我告诉每个我认识的患有癌症的人。

我的妈妈于 2006 年在爱达荷州被诊断出患有 1 期癌症。当时我是麻省理工学院的一名博士生，实验室的一位朋友帮助我在丹娜—法伯癌症研究所获得了预约。我认为这可能有点过分了（这是一种常见的癌症），但我们还是这么做了。他们说爱达荷州的一切都是标准护理，但建议进行一项额外的测试，爱达荷州团队随后不情愿地进行了这项测试，结果发现了远处转移（第四阶段！），极大地改变了她的治疗轨迹。她又活了 15 年（妈妈，我想你）。

寻求第二意见很糟糕。我们中的许多人从出生起就注定要信任我们的临床医生。但你即将踏上旅程，而你的生命（或你所爱之人的生命）正处于危险之中。保险通常会涵盖它。你的医生不会被冒犯。

这样想：如果你正在向火星探测器部署代码，而你的同事要求在你按下 go 之前进行代码审查，你会被冒犯吗？这比那更重要。

children.author: jcims
children.textRawHtml:
The second opinion thing has something I learned along the way. Get it BEFORE you have a treatment plan from the initial diagnosis. We got two second opinions (one for her first diagnosis and one for her recurrence) for my wife's ovarian cancer from Cleveland Clinic and MSK and in both cases the doctors would not advise/override the original doctor's treatment plan.

They were complete no-ops and a waste of time. Faced with that same situation today I would simply lie about whether or not a treatment plan was put into place.

Second bit of advice is to try as best you can to go into clinical trials with an understanding of the landscape of disqualifying treatments. Any immunotherapy treatment, for example, will disqualify you from nearly all subsequent clinical trials for immunotherapy.

Lastly the thing I would recommend for partners of loved ones in the crucible, don't get too distracted by trying to 'save the patient' that you miss opportunities stay connected with them in the process. It's not your responsibility to save their life, as much as it might feel that way when you're in the thick of it.
children.textZhHtml:
第二种观点是我一路走来学到的东西。 在您根据初步诊断制定治疗计划之前获取它。 对于我妻子的卵巢癌，我们从克利夫兰诊所和 MSK 得到了两份第二意见（一份针对她的第一次诊断，一份针对她的复发），在这两种情况下，医生都不会建议/推翻原来医生的治疗计划。

他们完全没有手术，浪费时间。 今天面对同样的情况，我会简单地谎报是否制定了治疗计划。

第二条建议是尽最大努力进入临床试验，了解不合格治疗的情况。 例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

最后，我向身处困境的亲人伴侣推荐的一件事是，不要因试图“拯救患者”而分心，从而错过在此过程中与他们保持联系的机会。 拯救他们的生命不是你的责任，尽管当你身处其中时可能会有这种感觉。

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
> Second bit of advice is to try as best you can to go into clinical trials with an understanding of the landscape of disqualifying treatments. Any immunotherapy treatment, for example, will disqualify you from nearly all subsequent clinical trials for immunotherapy.

While using this information for comparing clinical trials is fine, I want to emphasize that it would be phenomenally short-sighted to skip first-line approved immunotherapy in order to preserve the option for some random trial later on.

I'm not sure if you're actually suggesting this, but immunotherapies are some of the best cancer therapeutics that exist, so skipping approved drugs for future experiments is just a bad idea.
children.textZhHtml:
> 第二点建议是，在了解不合格治疗的情况的情况下，尽最大努力进行临床试验。例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去参加几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

虽然使用这些信息来比较临床试验没问题，但我想强调的是，为了保留以后进行一些随机试验的选择而跳过一线批准的免疫疗法是非常短视的。

我不确定您是否真的在暗示这一点，但免疫疗法是现有的最好的癌症疗法之一，因此在未来的实验中跳过已批准的药物是一个坏主意。

children.author: jcims
children.textRawHtml:
Well pointed out and I completely agree with your take.

In our case it was a clinical trial that the oncologist was aware of and we got in. I'd obviously heard of clinical trials but that was my introduction to the machinery by which they operate.
children.textZhHtml:
很好地指出，我完全同意你的看法。

在我们的案例中，这是一项肿瘤学家知道的临床试验，我们参与了。我显然听说过临床试验，但那是我对临床试验运作机制的介绍。

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
This may be a philosophical point of view, but I do not see much personal value in clinical trials. You're banking on there being a significant shift in technology/knowledge that occurs right between the time you are diagnosed and the time you have left to treat it. Just as a Bayesian probability, it's extremely unlikely to be the case.

Most studies that which reach stage 3 will not be approved, and that's because they're found to to be unhelpful or even harmful. So the most likely scenario is you do nothing or even hurt yourself by seeking out clinical studies, all of which will be optimistically framed as promising and potentially revolutionary. This can be particularly dangerous if you're opting into a trial in lieu of the standard treatment, as opposed to in addition to such.
children.textZhHtml:
这可能是一个哲学观点，但我在临床试验中没有看到太多个人价值。您指望在您被诊断出来和您剩下的治疗时间之间发生技术/知识的重大转变。正如贝叶斯概率一样，这种情况极不可能发生。

大多数达到第 3 阶段的研究都不会获得批准，这是因为它们被发现无益甚至有害。因此，最有可能的情况是，你什么都不做，甚至通过寻求临床研究来伤害自己，所有这些都将被乐观地认为是有前途的，并且具有潜在的革命性。如果您选择试验来代替标准治疗，而不是除此之外，这可能会特别危险。

children.author: akoboldfrying
children.textRawHtml:
> You're banking on there being a significant shift in technology/knowledge that occurs right between the time you are diagnosed and the time you have left to treat it. Just as a Bayesian probability, it's extremely unlikely to be the case.

The probability that I think you're talking about here is not actually relevant, given that the trial is already underway. Basically, the "potential advance" event has already happened. (Similarly, the probability of getting shot by an arrow is not relevant once the arrow's already poking out of your body.)

Given the trial is already underway, the probability that matters is the fraction of treatment candidates at the phase you are considering that make it all the way through; for phase 3 trials, this is 58-65% [0], which is actually pretty good. Of course, rates for earlier phases are much worse because there's attrition at each phase.

0: https://patentpc.com/blog/clinical-trial-success-rates-how-m...

考虑到试验已经在进行中，我认为您在这里谈论的概率实际上并不相关。基本上，“潜在提前”事件已经发生了。 （同样地，一旦箭已经从你的身体中射出，被箭射中的概率就不再重要了。）

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
A treatment being approved doesn't mean it's more effective than existing treatments, only that it is effective. And even then, not always as in the case of the controversial Alzheimer's drugs. Looking up some exact numbers on this, for oncology/cancer about 35% of treatments at stage 3 trials will end up approved/produced. [1] This [2] study looked at the 632 medicines approved (in the French market) and found that 25 ended up providing a substantial clinical benefit relative to existing treatments, so a bit under 4%. Even with just those two multipliers you're looking at around a 1% chance of the outcome most people are aiming for with trials.

[1] - https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/20/2/273/4817...

[2] - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660249/
children.textZhHtml:
一种疗法获得批准并不意味着它比现有疗法更有效，而只是意味着它确实有效。即便如此，情况也并不总是像备受争议的阿尔茨海默病药物那样。查一下这方面的一些确切数字，对于肿瘤学/癌症，大约 35% 的第三阶段试验治疗最终将获得批准/生产。 [1] 这项 [2] 研究考察了（在法国市场）批准的 632 种药物，发现其中 25 种最终相对于现有治疗方法提供了实质性的临床益处，因此略低于 4%。即使只有这两个乘数，大多数人通过试验获得的结果的可能性也只有 1%。

[1] - https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/20/2/273/4817...

[2] - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660249/

Yes this does increase that chance of shortsighted decisions or manipulation. children.textZhHtml:
这绝对是看待它的一种方式。

我只想说“危险”是相对的，当护理标准实际上没有希望时，您对风险的容忍度可能会改变。 是的，这确实增加了短视决策或操纵的可能性。 这只是领土带来的，我仍然非常感激我们可以选择参加这次活动。

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
The bigger problem with trials is not the danger, so much as the fact that they're unlikely to do anything.

As GP noted, most drugs don't work. To make it a bit more specific, even in phase 3, the failure rate for cancer drugs is something like 50%. And that's typically for some non-survival endpoint (assuming you even get the treatment, which is itself a coin flip).

Clinical trials are noble, admirable things to do, but too many people think of them as treatments, when they really are not. They're an experiment that you do with your body when you reach the end of the road and there are no more options.

It always makes me a little sad to hear how patients talk about trials and fight to get into them, as if being in the trial is somehow progress. Expectations are not being managed properly.
children.textZhHtml:
试验的更大问题不是危险，而是试验不太可能起任何作用。

正如全科医生指出的那样，大多数药物都不起作用。更具体地说，即使在第三阶段，抗癌药物的失败率也约为 50%。这通常是为了一些非生存终点（假设你甚至得到了治疗，这本身就是抛硬币）。

临床试验是崇高、令人钦佩的事情，但太多人认为它们是治疗，而实际上并非如此。这是当你到达路的尽头并且没有更多选择时，你用自己的身体做的一个实验。

听到病人如何谈论试验并努力参加试验，总是让我有点难过，好像参加试验就是某种进步。期望没有得到适当的管理。

children.author: jcims
children.textRawHtml:
>The bigger problem with trials is not the danger, so much as the fact that they're unlikely to do anything.

And? What is the point of this observation? Of course they are unlikely to do anything. Your other option is to do nothing and die. Nothing wrong with that if that's what people choose to do...'accept their fate' and all that. I'm not opposed to it at all, there's a certain appeal to it.

But when your wife and the mother of your two beautiful daughters is laying helpless on nature's altar you fucking move dude. You don't do nothing.
children.textZhHtml:
>试验的更大问题不是危险，而是他们不太可能做任何事情。

然后呢？ 这个观察有什么意义呢？ 当然，他们不太可能做任何事情。 你的另一个选择就是什么都不做然后死去。 如果这就是人们选择做的事……“接受他们的命运”之类的，那就没有错。 我一点也不反对，它有一定的吸引力。

但是当你的妻子和你两个漂亮女儿的母亲无助地躺在大自然的祭坛上时，你他妈的感动了伙计。 你什么也不做。

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
The point is exactly what I said: “doing something”, in this case, is not the same thing as “saving your loved one’s life.”

> Your other option is to do nothing and die

I really don’t want to be this blunt, but I don’t know how to say it any other way: death is not an option. When you’re at the stage of clinical trials for cancer therapies, it is the inevitable outcome. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be in the trial. Maybe it extends the inevitable, maybe it doesn’t. The odds lean heavily toward the latter. And there’s also always a cost.

I’ve lost friends and family to cancer too, and watching people you love torture themselves with ineffective (or even minimally effective) treatments is agonizing.

When it comes to clinical trials, you need to start with the cold, hard reality that you’re doing an altruistic experiment with the remaining portion of your life. There are lot of people who don’t understand that, and see trials as some kind of back-door to better treatment.
children.textZhHtml:
重点就是我所说的：在这种情况下，“做某事”与“拯救你所爱的人的生命”不是一回事。

>你的另一个选择是什么都不做然后死去

我真的不想这么直白，但我不知道如何用其他方式表达：死亡不是一种选择。当您处于癌症治疗的临床试验阶段时，这是不可避免的结果。否则，你就不会参加审判。也许它延长了不可避免的事情，也许不是。可能性严重倾向于后者。而且总是要付出代价的。

我也因癌症失去了朋友和家人，看着你所爱的人用无效（甚至微乎其微）的治疗来折磨自己是令人痛苦的。

当谈到临床试验时，你需要从冷酷、残酷的现实开始，你正在用你生命的剩余部分做一场利他主义的实验。很多人不明白这一点，并将试验视为更好治疗的某种后门。

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
Not that long ago I went to see an acquaintance during his last time on this Earth - bladder cancer. His final time would come the next afternoon, so he was already well into the 'he can hear you but can't speak' phase. At first I felt absolutely awful for him and in general. But then thinking about it more I realized that there's nothing to really feel particularly bad about.

In not that long I'll be the one laying there in that bed, and so will everybody else that was in that room, and even on this Earth. It's just a natural part of life. He, at least, had the privilege of being able to prepare for his final moments, and getting to spend it surrounded by friends and loved ones. It's the final scene that we all will go through, one way or the other. And you know, that's about as ideal a closing act as one could hope for.

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
I agree. And people who have been through it frequently (e.g. doctors) have a completely different reaction to those who are going through it for the first time. But still, it's understandably a sensitive subject, and even the person most inured to death reacts differently when it's their own family (or themselves) who is dealing with it.

That said, the folks who are recruiting for clinical trials are often playing on this emotional reaction, and over-promising what can be accomplished, or simply not correcting the misperceptions of the people they are recruiting.

It's hard to recruit people into trials when you tell them with absolute clarity that there's very little chance it will benefit them personally.

children.author: citizenpaul
children.textRawHtml: I lost somone to a rare cancer with almost zero chance of survival.  A treatment with 65% success was available 30 days after they died.  Ill always wonder if things could have been different. Maybe if we looked harder for trials but like you we thought it a hopeless waste of the limited time left.

children.author: abirch
children.textRawHtml: I’m sorry for your loss. Words from an internet rando don’t mean much, but you did the best that you could so don’t worry about what ifs. Do your best right now.
children.textZhHtml: 对于您的损失，我深表歉意。网络随机的话没有多大意义，但你已经尽力了，所以不用担心如果发生什么。现在就尽力而为。

comments.author: OsrsNeedsf2P
comments.textRawHtml:
DS isn't better than Sol and Gemini in the benchmarks, but after working with them all for a while now I'm beginning to understand why people find DS _feels_ so much better.

First, it's the tok/s and TTFT from providers. Deepseek blazes through work - at quite good quality - and you don't find yourself waiting for your agents to finish.

Second is the openness. Being able to see the CoT and not being randomly blocked for cyber review. You're never wondering if it's stuck or if it will randomly fail. Combined with the great cost value.. My next subscription will probably be Z.ai

children.author: Philip-J-Fry
children.textRawHtml:
Feels better to me in the sense that it doesn't try to be too clever. When I ask it to do things it actually generates code that a developer would write. That still lets me build software in layers like I do mentally. And it keeps you in control of where abstractions are.

Some people would say that you don't need this at all with the frontier llms. But when extending existing software or writing software that fits into an existing ecosystem, I find I still need to offer a lot of guidance. And it's better that the context window isn't flooded with code that was reverted after I looked at it.

Given how expensive this computation would have been in 1997, it makes perfect sense they'd taken months, but even if we assume they tried all timestamps of 1997 and selected arbitrarily among the first 16 viable candidate of any timestamp, that's just ~30 bits of freedom.

Finding out there is a class of weak 256-bit elliptic curves so large that they can be hit randomly with 2^30 tries would be a cryptanalytic breakthrough analogous to discovering all elliptic curve cryptography is broken.

Almost all of the smaller values of n are not valid curve values, so they were searching "harder" but just for valid seeds. If you look at the generator output in [1], you'll see that:

children.author: etempleton
children.textRawHtml:
This has been my argument for the past few weeks to explain why we aren’t seeing or feeling real world productivity gains as consumers despite many espousing the efficiency of AI they personally see with their own workflows. The hands on work is rarely the actual bottleneck.

My team can crank out high quality work in a few hours and AI could do the same medium to high quality work in a minute or two, but the review, feedback, and sign off takes days of back and forth. AI just slows this part of the process down because editing AI work is often a challenge because, no one is quite as familiar with how it was put together and sometimes it creates things that are not editable at all. And telling AI to make very specific changes is often a mixed bag at best.

Solo devs and small teams with minimal oversight can probably move a lot faster, but corporations are going to see minimal uplift except in areas where no one is looking.
children.textZhHtml:
这一直是我在过去几周的论点，以解释为什么我们作为消费者没有看到或感受到现实世界的生产力提高，尽管许多人拥护他们亲眼所见的人工智能在自己的工作流程中的效率。动手工作很少是真正的瓶颈。

我的团队可以在几个小时内完成高质量的工作，人工智能可以在一两分钟内完成相同的中等到高质量的工作，但审查、反馈和签署需要几天的时间来回。人工智能只是减慢了这部分过程，因为编辑人工智能工作通常是一项挑战，因为没有人非常熟悉它是如何组合在一起的，有时它会创建根本无法编辑的东西。告诉人工智能做出非常具体的改变往往是一个好坏参半的问题。

独立开发者和监督最少的小团队可能会移动得更快，但除了无人关注的领域之外，企业将看到最小的提升。

children.author: majormajor
children.textRawHtml:
Established successful companies operate in a world where action and change often introduce more immediate risk than staying still. In those companies AI doesn't necessarily offer a lot of "increased productivity" gains because writing the code isn't the bottleneck. But many of them will try to chase cost savings by laying people off or slowing hiring.

There's a couple types of companies where the reverse is true: young companies trying to grow, and dying ones that need a turnaround.

Out of those two, young companies are less likely to be set in their ways. So the first place you really see the result of development moving faster with AI is probably going to be in future months and years when suddenly-big companies start getting widely known with products and business strategies that wouldn't have made sense a decade ago because writing code to try different things to even get the ball rolling was a bottleneck, and you could only do things that wouldn't scale for so long.
children.textZhHtml:
对于成熟的成功公司来说，行动和变革往往比保持静止会带来更直接的风险。在这些公司中，人工智能不一定会带来很多“提高生产力”的收益，因为编写代码并不是瓶颈。但他们中的许多人会试图通过裁员或放慢招聘速度来节省成本。

有几种类型的公司情况恰恰相反：年轻的公司试图发展，而垂死的公司需要扭亏为盈。

在这两种公司中，年轻的公司不太可能按自己的方式行事。因此，你第一个真正看到 AI 带来的更快发展的结果可能是在未来的几个月和几年里，那时大公司突然开始以十年前没有意义的产品和业务策略而广为人知，因为编写代码来尝试不同的事情甚至让事情滚动是一个瓶颈，你只能做一些无法长期扩展的事情。

Yeah, it's very confusing especially if you're not in the loop and their docs were only updated recently and was confusing during the v1 -> v2 transition weeks / months ago.

So far, "OpenCode" has gone through several possible definitions:

- OpenCode Terminal / CLI - This is what you get normally. Runs a service in the background and the CLI is your interface.

- OpenCode Desktop - Instead of a CLI, you get a desktop interface.

Most users usually stop here. You just install the app and you connect wherever.

So there's the services where they both make money and make things easier for users:

- OpenCode Console - Basically the serving platform for both Zen and Go, and has expanded to a hosted inference gateway and somewhat similar to OpenRouter or a managed LiteLLM. Has the option to BYOK if you have existing AI platform accounts so it charges those instead of Zen, and that's what got compromised.

- OpenCode Zen - the API service they host if you want to get access to providers but don't want to pay individually per API platform. Similar to OpenRouter. I noticed they're kinda slowly dropping the Zen moniker.

- OpenCode Go - the subscription service that they host that features open weight models and select low-cost models from frontier labs. Has different policies when it comes to privacy and retention compared to Zen.

- OpenCode Black - a limited-time, limited access subscription service that grants access to frontier models. Not sure if this is still alive or not.

comments.author: antasvara
comments.textRawHtml:
Nathan Fielder is pretty well-known for his work in The Rehearsal and Nathan for You. Nathan for You resides in the docu-comedy genre, where you take advantage of real people's reactions to absurd situations for comedic effect. Other examples are things like Kitchen Nightmares (where Gordon Ramsey goes into real restaurants and "fixes" them). It's a well-done version of the idea, but not revolutionary IMO.

The Rehearsal, however, extends the idea further. In that show, he helps real people "rehearse" for hard conversations. It involves Fielder building extravagant sets and having absurdly detailed set-ups with multiple actors, then running the conversation multiple times. What makes this "different" is that now the real person is partially in on it? Like, they know that they're on a set. They know that this is a simulation. So the show is more "meta" than previous entries in the genre, opening up other avenues for humour.

I say this because You Can See Everything is best understood as a further extension of those projects. Even the name indicates this, because by nature of a documentary, you can't see everything. You have a real person in Elizabeth Holmes, being interviewed by a person in Fielder that's known for his stunts taking advantage of "real people," where he watches fictionalized versions of Holmes with Holmes herself? Viewed in light of his previous projects, this feels like an extension of them.

But even with that, I think the setup does allow you to see something real in Holmes. She also knows how people "want" to see her! So there's also a sort of meta-narrative there too, where you know Holmes is on her best behavior to try and dispel the narrative from those fictionalized TV characterizations. The fact that she comes off poorly in the documentary says something, even accounting for the fact that Fielder is trying to sell a narrative.

It's a real mind game, but I think it's representative of Holmes because of that. She is going to jail for a fraud that amounts to a similar sort of mind game, she agrees to a documentary to show herself differently, but that documentary is also a mind game. Wild stuff.

stories.title: How the Claude Code team does code review

comments.author: avinoth
comments.textRawHtml:
This is like one of Google’s infrastructure blog. Google scale things are only relevant and appropriate for them. We had lots of bitter lessons from smaller engineering teams following the process with the justification that “this is how Google does it”.

Similarly, Anthropic can afford to do this because they have virtually unlimited tokens and labs to train models for their specific usecase. The rest of us need code comprehension lest we become dependent on continuous supply of tokens (which is a state these labs badly want to achieve)

So, unless you work at a lab, or have unlimited tokens guaranteed through the life of your company, it would do both the company and you good to continue to read the code and not let these 30k PRs per engineer be the norm.

An excerpt from the article makes my point

> Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
comments.textZhHtml:
这就像 Google 的基础设施博客之一。谷歌规模的东西只与他们相关并且适合他们。我们从较小的工程团队那里吸取了很多惨痛的教训，他们遵循的过程是“谷歌就是这样做的”。

同样，Anthropic 也有能力做到这一点，因为他们拥有几乎无限的代币和实验室来训练针对其特定用例的模型。我们其他人需要代码理解，以免我们变得依赖于持续供应代币（这是这些实验室非常希望实现的状态）

因此，除非您在实验室工作，或者在公司的整个生命周期内保证拥有无限的代币，否则继续阅读代码而不是让每个工程师 30k PR 成为常态，对公司和您都有好处。

文章的摘录表明了我的观点

>团队成员的头脑中保留着 Claude Code 的完整心理模型，我们认为任何人都不需要这样做。当有人想要理解代码库的一部分时，他们会要求 Claude 为该部分编写一个解释器。它需要几分钟的时间并反映当前的代码。

They pretty much fixed that. Plus you can influence the writing style to some extent. I tell it to use full sentences and avoid assuming I already understand the code.

Another thing is that it's very good at creating diagrams (I think someone wrote a skill for it so maybe not by default). I usually find the diagrams are even more valuable than the text.

Honestly I was skeptical but you really can just point Claude at some code and ask it to make a markdown + SVG explainer and it will do a shockingly good job.

I'd still rather read human documentation, but even before AI almost nobody writes any - especially for internal code. And they certainly don't make great diagrams.
